Conceptual Physics — Unit 1 — Forces, Motion, and Equilibrium

Canonical Unit Bank. Student-facing content is separated from teacher keys. Secure content must not be exposed in instructional resources.

Unit Mastery Goals

  • U1-MG01 — Use evidence and models to distinguish observations, inferences, and testable physics explanations, and communicate what a representation or relationship means.
  • U1-MG02 — Explain Newton’s First Law and inertia to predict when an object’s motion remains unchanged or changes.
  • U1-MG03 — Represent and determine net force using vectors, then use the result to classify balanced and unbalanced situations.
  • U1-MG04 — Create, critique, and defend force models for real-world systems using evidence about interactions and motion.

WTC

Section 1.1: Thinking Like a Physicist

U1-S1-WTC01 What's To Come DOK 2 instructional

A student changes only pendulum length and records the time for five swings. Study the measurement plot. Before deciding why the pattern occurs, write one statement that is directly supported by the measurements and one question that could be tested next.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: A supported statement should describe the measured pattern without adding an unmeasured cause; a testable question should name a measurable change and outcome.

Solution / rationale: Example: “Longer pendulums in this set took more time for five swings.” Testable question: “If the pendulum length is increased beyond 60 cm, does the time for five swings continue to increase?”

Mastery Goal
U1-MG01
Learning Target
Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.
I Can
I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.

Section 1.2: Forces and Newton’s First Law

U1-S2-WTC01 What's To Come DOK 2 instructional

A hockey puck glides across nearly frictionless ice. Imagine every horizontal interaction could suddenly disappear. Predict what the puck would do next, then name the idea you would need in order to defend that prediction after this section.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: It would continue at constant velocity in a straight line; Newton’s First Law/inertia explains the prediction.

Section 1.4: Equilibrium and Balanced Motion

U1-S4-WTC01 What's To Come DOK 2 instructional

Two objects have zero net force. Object A is sitting on a shelf. Object B is already moving east. Predict what can be true about B’s motion while its net force stays zero. Be ready to revisit your answer after the section.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: B can continue east at constant speed in a straight line; zero net force does not require rest.

Section 1.5: Modeling Forces in the Real World

U1-S5-WTC01 What's To Come DOK 3 instructional

A force model for a book resting on a table shows only a downward weight arrow. The modeler claims, “The diagram is complete because gravity is the only force that matters.” Record one piece of motion evidence that the completed model must account for and one question you would ask about the missing interactions.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: Evidence: the book remains at rest, so its net force is zero. A useful question asks what upward interaction from the table balances weight.

Section 1.1: Thinking Like a Physicist

U1-S1-NOTE-EX01 Notes DOK 2 instructional

Example — Observation or inference? A metal spoon is placed in hot water. After 30 s, its handle is warmer than before. Separate what was directly observed from one reasonable inference.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: Observation: the handle became warmer after 30 s. Inference: energy was transferred through the spoon from the hotter region toward the cooler handle.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: Observation: the thermometer reading increased from 22°C to 29°C. Inference: the contents gained thermal energy or sunlight contributed to warming; the inference goes beyond the measured values.

Example — Evidence and explanation. Trial data for a toy car are stopping distances of 2.1 m, 2.0 m, and 2.2 m on surface A and 0.8 m, 0.9 m, and 0.8 m on surface B. Which claim is better supported: “surface A resists the motion less” or “the car has more inertia on surface A”? Explain.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: The first claim is better supported because the same car travels farther on A before stopping. The data compare the surfaces; they do not show that the car’s inertia changed.

Section 1.2: Forces and Newton’s First Law

U1-S2-NOTE-EX01 Notes DOK 2 instructional

Example — Newton’s First Law. A cart moves east at constant velocity while the horizontal forces on it balance. Explain why no extra “motion force” is needed to keep it moving.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: Newton’s First Law says an object continues with constant velocity when net force is zero. Motion does not require a net forward force; a net force is required to change velocity.

Example — Inertia is not a force. When a bus stops suddenly, a passenger’s body tends to keep moving forward. Explain the event using inertia without inventing an “inertia force.”

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: The passenger’s body resists a change in velocity and tends to continue forward. The seat or seat belt must exert a force to change that motion; inertia itself is a property of matter, not a force.

Section 1.3: Net Force and Vectors

U1-S3-NOTE-EX01 Notes DOK 2 instructional

Example — Vector meaning. A 6 N arrow points east and a 10 N arrow points east. Explain how the arrow directions and lengths determine the resultant.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: Because the forces point in the same direction, their magnitudes add. The resultant is 16 N east, represented by an eastward arrow longer than either original arrow.

Section 1.4: Equilibrium and Balanced Motion

U1-S4-NOTE-EX01 Notes DOK 2 instructional

Example — Static equilibrium. A lamp hangs motionless from a vertical cord. Its weight is 45 N. Use the equilibrium rule to determine the cord tension.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: Because $\Sigma F=0$, the upward tension must equal the 45 N downward weight. Tension = 45 N upward.

Mastery Goal
U1-MG02|U1-MG03
Learning Target

U1-S5-NOTE-EX01 Notes DOK 2 instructional

Example — Choose the system first. For a book resting on a table, make the book the system. Which forces belong on the book’s force diagram, and which tempting force does not belong?

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: Include Earth’s gravitational force on the book and the table’s support force on the book. Do not include the force the book exerts on the table because that force acts on the table, not on the chosen system.

Example — Connect evidence to a model. A sled moves straight at constant speed while being pulled. The model shows pull right, friction left, support up, and weight down. What must be true about the paired magnitudes?

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: Pull and friction must balance horizontally; support and weight must balance vertically. Then the net force is zero, consistent with constant velocity.

Which statement is an observation rather than an inference? A student records: A thermometer reads 31.2°C. Choose the statement that stays closest to what was directly measured.

  1. A thermometer reads 31.2°C.
  2. The equipment worked perfectly.
  3. The liquid gained energy.
  4. The cause of the result is already proven.
Teacher key and metadata

Answer: A. A thermometer reads 31.2°C.

  4. A law is an untested guess and a theory is a fact.
Teacher key and metadata

U1-S1-PS2-Q12 Practice Set 2 DOK 2 instructional

Why is the statement “The magnet works because nature prefers attraction.” weak as a scientific explanation?

  1. A claim is scientific whenever most people agree with it.
  2. It does not identify a measurable, testable mechanism or relationship.
  3. It contains too few numerical values.
  4. Scientific explanations must always be equations.
Teacher key and metadata

Answer: B. It does not identify a measurable, testable mechanism or relationship.

  2. A model is an exact copy of reality with every detail included.

  4. A model is a simplified representation used to describe, explain, or predict aspects of a system.

Answer: A. A law describes a consistent relationship or pattern; a theory explains how or why phenomena occur and is supported by evidence.

U1-S2-PS2-Q05 Practice Set 2 DOK 3 instructional

A classmate makes a Newton’s First Law claim. a student writes, “The cart keeps moving because the original push is still stored inside it.” Critique and revise the explanation using Newton’s First Law.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: The object tends to maintain its previous velocity because of inertia. A real interaction must act on it to change that velocity while the skateboard slows.

U1-S4-PS3-Q05 Practice Set 3 DOK 2 instructional

A student is checking whether a motion claim is consistent with $\Sigma F=0$. A car moves around a circular track at constant speed. Is it in mechanical equilibrium?

  1. Yes, because constant speed always means zero net force.
  2. No, because all moving objects are unbalanced.
  3. No, because its velocity direction changes, so a net force is required.
  4. Yes, because equilibrium means only that speed is unchanged.
Teacher key and metadata

Answer: C. No, because its velocity direction changes, so a net force is required.

A force diagram is drawn for a shopping cart, but one arrow represents “the cart pushing on the shopper.” What is the modeling error?

  1. That force acts on the shopper, not on the chosen cart system.
  2. Forces exerted by objects are never real.
  3. Every diagram must include all action-reaction pairs on one object.
  4. Only gravitational forces belong on force diagrams.
Teacher key and metadata

Answer: A. That force acts on the shopper, not on the chosen cart system.

A force model and motion evidence disagree. What should a physicist do first?

  1. Check the chosen system, missing/extra interactions, arrow directions/magnitudes, and the observations before revising the model.
  2. Keep the model because diagrams are always more reliable than observations.

  4. Add an inertia force until the diagram matches.

During a force-model audit, what is the best reason to label the chosen system before drawing a force diagram?

  1. It guarantees every force will be balanced.
  2. It removes the need to identify interaction partners.

Answer: C. It determines which interactions count as forces acting on the object being modeled.

U1-S5-PS3-Q01 Practice Set 3 DOK 2 instructional

A student is checking whether a diagram matches its chosen system and motion evidence. A force diagram is drawn for a shopping cart, but one arrow represents “the cart pushing on the shopper.” What is the modeling error?

  1. That force acts on the shopper, not on the chosen cart system.
  2. Only gravitational forces belong on force diagrams.
  3. Every diagram must include all action-reaction pairs on one object.
  4. Forces exerted by objects are never real.
Teacher key and metadata

Answer: A. That force acts on the shopper, not on the chosen cart system.

Answer: (a) Model A. Constant velocity requires zero horizontal net force. (b) Evidence that the crate is speeding up in the forward direction (or otherwise changing velocity forward) would make a forward resultant plausible.

U1-S5-PS3-Q12 Practice Set 3 DOK 3 instructional

A student is checking whether a diagram matches its chosen system and motion evidence. A student claims a stationary object has “no forces because nothing happens.” Build a brief CER-style response for a supported object at rest: state a claim, identify evidence, and connect the evidence to net force.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: Claim: forces can act on a stationary object and be balanced. Evidence: the object remains at rest while gravity and a support interaction are present. Reasoning: unchanged velocity is consistent with $\Sigma F=0$, so the forces cancel rather than disappear.

Write a two-sentence defense of a force model: sentence 1 identifies the net force; sentence 2 connects that result to the observed motion. Use a scenario in which a cart is at rest with balanced forces.

Answer: Example: “The force arrows sum to zero, so the cart’s net force is 0 N. That result is consistent with the observed unchanged velocity of zero.”

U1-S2-ETA-Q01 Exit Ticket A DOK 2 formative-secure

A cart moves east at constant velocity while two horizontal forces act on it. What must be true about the vector sum of those horizontal forces? Explain with Newton’s First Law.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: The horizontal vector sum is zero. Constant velocity means no change in velocity, so Newton’s First Law requires zero net force.

Performance

Performance Task

U1-PERF01 Performance Task DOK 3-4 secure

Performance Task — Low-Resistance Cart Evidence. A team gives a cart one brief push, then stops touching it. They record velocity at equal 1 s intervals after release on two tracks.

Track S (smooth): 0.82, 0.80, 0.79, 0.78, 0.76 m/s.
Track R (rough): 0.82, 0.67, 0.52, 0.36, 0.21 m/s.

(a) Identify one observation from the data and one inference about horizontal interactions.
(b) For each track, sketch or describe a force model after the push has ended, including weight, support, and any important horizontal force.
(c) Decide which track more closely approximates the zero-horizontal-net-force condition used in Newton’s First Law and defend the decision with data.
(d) A teammate says, “The cart on Track S keeps moving because the original push remains inside it.” Critique and revise this explanation.
(e) Name one limitation of using these data as evidence for an ideal zero-net-force model.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: See complete teacher solution.

Solution / rationale: (a) Observation example: on Track S the measured speed changes only from 0.82 to 0.76 m/s, while Track R changes from 0.82 to 0.21 m/s. Inference: the horizontal resistive interaction is smaller on Track S.
(b) Both models include weight down and support up. After contact ends there is no continuing applied push. Track S should show a small leftward resistive force (or an explicitly noted approximation of negligible resistance); Track R should show a larger leftward resistive force.
(c) Track S more closely approximates zero horizontal net force because its velocity remains much closer to constant over the same interval. The 0.06 m/s decrease is much smaller than the 0.61 m/s decrease on Track R.
(d) The push is an interaction that ended when contact ended; it is not stored as a force. The cart continues because of inertia, and with a small net force its velocity changes only slightly.
(e) Examples: Track S still has some resistance; measurement uncertainty is not reported; only a short time interval and one set of trials are shown. Repeated trials would strengthen the evidence.

Expected evidence: MG01: distinguish observation/inference and evaluate evidence; MG02: connect near-zero net force with nearly unchanged velocity and correct inertia language; MG04: create/defend force models and identify limitations.

Scoring notes: Score parts separately with the course progress language. Meeting requires scientifically coherent data use, force models on the cart system, and Newton’s First Law reasoning. Exceeding may include a strong limitation/uncertainty analysis or a particularly clear model-data defense.

U1-PERF02 Performance Task DOK 3-4 secure

Performance Task — Model Audit at a Loading Dock. A powered cart moves a crate across a level floor. During one 4 s interval, video markers show the crate moves in a straight line with equal 1.5 m spacing each second. A student proposes this force model for the crate: weight 90 N down, support 90 N up, drive interaction 28 N right, friction 18 N left, and “motion force” 10 N right.

(a) Use the motion evidence to classify the crate’s motion during the interval.
(b) Compute the horizontal resultant of the student’s listed arrows. Explain whether that resultant agrees with the motion evidence.
(c) Identify every modeling error or unsupported feature you can justify, then revise the horizontal model so it matches the evidence.
(d) Defend the revised model using Newton’s First Law and the equilibrium rule.
(e) Suppose later video markers become farther apart each second while the crate still moves right. Describe one physically consistent change to the horizontal force model.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: See complete teacher solution.

Solution / rationale: (a) Equal spacing in equal time along a straight line indicates constant velocity.
(b) The listed horizontal arrows give 28 N right + 10 N right - 18 N left = 20 N right. A 20 N right resultant predicts changing velocity, so it conflicts with the constant-velocity evidence.
(c) “Motion force” is not an interaction and should be removed. The remaining 28 N drive and 18 N friction still give 10 N right, so at least one magnitude is inconsistent with this interval if these are the only horizontal forces. A revised model can use 18 N right drive and 18 N left friction, or 28 N right drive and 28 N left total resistance, while preserving balanced 90 N vertical forces.
(d) The revised force model has $\Sigma F_x=0$ and $\Sigma F_y=0$, so $\Sigma F=0$. Newton’s First Law therefore predicts constant velocity, which matches the video evidence.
(e) Farther spacing means the crate speeds up to the right, so the revised horizontal resultant must point right; for example, drive could increase above friction or friction could decrease while drive stays the same.

Expected evidence: MG02: constant velocity/N1L; MG03: net-force arithmetic and equilibrium; MG04: critique, revise, and defend a force model.

Scoring notes: Meeting requires correct motion interpretation, net-force calculation, removal of the invalid motion-force idea, and a balanced revised model. Exceeding includes a precise defense connecting representation, evidence, and law.

Answer: Inertia is a property of matter, not a force. The object tends to preserve its velocity; an actual interaction force is required to change that velocity. Newton’s First Law describes the zero-net-force case.

Expected evidence: Secure evidence for U1-MG02: Explain Newton’s First Law and inertia to predict when an object’s motion remains unchanged or changes.

U1-SUM-V6-Q08 Summative DOK 2 secure

A student must choose between two claims for a probe: Claim A—engines must run to maintain constant speed; Claim B—zero net force is sufficient for constant velocity. Which claim is consistent with Newton’s First Law and why?

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: Claim B. Constant velocity is maintained when net force is zero; a continuing thrust would create a velocity change unless balanced.

Expected evidence: Secure evidence for U1-MG02: Explain Newton’s First Law and inertia to predict when an object’s motion remains unchanged or changes.

Scoring notes: Selected response: 1 point. Constructed response: full credit requires correct physics and the requested reasoning/representation; partial credit for a correct core idea with a limited omission.

U1-SUM-V6-Q09 Summative DOK 3 secure

A model of a book at rest shows support 40 N up and weight 30 N down. Motion evidence says the book remains at rest. (a) Identify the mismatch. (b) Give two possible model checks or revisions.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: The model has 10 N up net force, inconsistent with rest. Recheck measured/represented force magnitudes, include any missing downward interaction if physically present, or revise support/weight so the total is zero if those are the only forces.

Expected evidence: Secure evidence for U1-MG04: Create, critique, and defend force models for real-world systems using evidence about interactions and motion.

Scoring notes: Selected response: 1 point. Constructed response: full credit requires correct physics and the requested reasoning/representation; partial credit for a correct core idea with a limited omission.

U1-SUM-V6-Q10 Summative DOK 3 secure

A 10 N resultant points northeast and one perpendicular component is 6 N east. Determine the magnitude and direction of the other perpendicular component.

Teacher key and metadata

Answer: The other component is 8 N north because $6^2+8^2=10^2$.

Expected evidence: Secure evidence for U1-MG03: Represent and determine net force using vectors, then use the result to classify balanced and unbalanced situations.

Scoring notes: Selected response: 1 point. Constructed response: full credit requires correct physics and the requested reasoning/representation; partial credit for a correct core idea with a limited omission.
